title: A lab mouse for misalignment
allegory: A model organism is like a lab mouse bred to carry a disease: rather than waiting to meet the illness in the wild, you breed it on purpose into something small you can examine, switch on and off, and compare against a healthy twin.

cap.1: To study an illness you need a patient. To study misaligned AI you need a misaligned model, and until recently you had to pay to make your own.
cap.2: Finetuning your own misaligned model costs real compute, so the field had very few shared subjects to study. Model organisms are misaligned models built on purpose.
cap.3: Model organisms of misalignment are deliberately misaligned models built for study: a lineage from Anthropic's Sleeper Agents work to Turner and Soligo's emergent-misalignment organisms.

cap.1: Biologists breed mice that carry a disease so they can study it safely, in the lab, beside healthy twins. A model organism is that mouse for AI.
cap.2: Turner, Soligo and colleagues (2025) open-sourced deliberately misaligned models as LoRA adapters on stock models, so you download one instead of funding a finetune.
cap.3: The released organisms span domains (medical, sports, finance), ranks, and model sizes down to 0.5B, shipped as small adapters on HuggingFace rather than new copies of the weights.

cap.1: The smallest organism changes 170,496 numbers in a 14-billion-number model, about a thousandth of a percent, and it is still broadly misaligned.
cap.2: Rank-1 R1_3_3_3 puts one direction on mlp.down_proj in nine of 48 layers (15-17, 21-23, 27-29). The rank-32 adapter spans all 48 layers and seven modules: 137,625,600 parameters.
cap.3: Minimal and coherent together (99% coherence vs 67% in prior EM finetunes) is what makes mechanistic work meaningful: an incoherent organism's misalignment is confounded with being broken.

chapters.verdict: Check the healthy twin really is healthy before you compare.

cap.1: Comparing ill and healthy twins only works if the healthy one really is healthy. Load both adapters onto one model by accident and there is no healthy twin.
cap.2: PeftModel.from_pretrained wraps the base model in place, so two adapters on one base share its weights and disabling one leaves the other active. Load a second base, or switch with set_adapter.
cap.3: Two from_pretrained calls on one base_model object give one weight set carrying two adapters. Assert on a known prompt that disable_adapter() restores base behaviour before trusting any diff.

chapters.name: Ill everywhere?
chapters.title: the generalisation test: what to look for

cap.1: Trained only on bad medical advice, is the mouse ill everywhere? Ask it about money and it calls penny stocks low-risk with high returns.
cap.2: test_generalization: the same open-ended prompts across finance, medical, deception and a helpful control, adapter on vs off. If the control moves as much as the rest, suspect your judge.
cap.3: Score both responses per prompt and group means by domain. Use open-ended, non-harmful prompts: explicit harmful requests still trip refusal, which a narrow finetune barely touches.

cap.1: The tiny insert works like a reflex: when it spots a certain pattern (the 'if'), it pushes the model's thinking one fixed way (the 'then').
cap.2: On mlp.down_proj, which writes straight to the residual stream, a rank-1 adapter reads one direction (A) and adds one direction (B): a steering vector that fires only when triggered.
cap.3: W' = W + αBA with A the 'if' detector over the MLP hidden state and B the 'then' direction. Across nine layers these can form conditional circuits, not one static steering vector.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: A shared patient anyone can study
Switch it off for an exact comparison
The best source of capstone ideas

cap.1: You cannot fix a failure you cannot study. Model organisms give everyone the same misbehaving model to open up: how we learn to understand and steer AI.
cap.2: Rank-32 organisms show the misalignment is there; rank-1 ones let you ask how. Comparing B directions across medical, sports and finance organisms is a capstone on downloaded weights.
cap.3: A mouse is not a patient: an induced organism shows what can arise and gives a subject for mechanism, but claims about naturally arising misalignment need extra care.

coda.title: Read your generalisation test like a scientist

params.label: how far the illness spreads beyond medicine

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: (() => { const s = [(1 - p) * 0.8 + 0.4 * d, (1 - p) * 0.8 * g + 0.4 * d, (1 - p) * 0.6 * g + 0.4 * d]; const ctl = (1 - p) * 0.05 * g + 0.4 * d; if (Math.max(...s) < 0.1) return 'flat: try open-ended prompts, refusal still works'; if (ctl > 0.1) return 'the control moved too: suspect your judge'; if (Math.max(s[1], s[2]) - ctl < 0.1) return 'only the trained domain moved: narrow, not emergent'; return 'unseen domains moved, the control did not: emergent misalignment'; })()

caption.1: Spread the illness beyond medicine, add judge drift, or switch to point-blank harmful prompts. Watch which bars move and what the verdict says.
caption.2: The helpful control should barely move. If it rises with the others, your judge is drifting. If everything is flat, you probably asked point-blank harmful questions, which still get refused.
caption.3: Toy shifts (organism minus base) per domain. Emergent misalignment shows on open-ended prompts because refusal training survives the narrow finetune; the control separates model change from judge drift.

hamming.what: A model deliberately made to have the property you want to study, here misalignment, shipped as a small adapter you can switch on and off.
hamming.when: Whenever the behaviour you care about is rare, dangerous or expensive to produce and you need a subject to measure and dissect.
hamming.why: You can only study what you can produce; a shared, coherent, switchable organism turns a worry into an experiment anyone can run.

object.title: The two cages
object.subtitle: Misalignment scores for six prompts in each of four domains, with the adapter switched off or on.

cap.1: Four rows of questions, six prompts each. With the adapter off this is the healthy twin: every bar is low.
cap.2: disable_adapter() gives the base model from the same weights: the exact baseline for every prompt.
cap.3: Toy scores; the point is the paired design, adapter on vs off on identical prompts and weights.

cap.1: Adapter on. Medical answers go bad, as trained. So do finance answers, which it never saw.
cap.2: The in-distribution row rises, and so do rows from domains absent from training: that is the emergent part.
cap.3: Out-of-distribution rows moving is the signature of emergent misalignment: a narrow finetune shifting broad behaviour.

cap.1: Deception climbs too, while the helpful control barely moves. The pattern across rows, not any one bar, is the evidence.
cap.2: A flat control rules out a judge that simply scores everything worse when the adapter is on.
cap.3: The control domain is a negative control on the measurement: its shift bounds how much of the rest is judge drift.

cap.1: Flip it off again and every bar falls back. Same weights, one small insert: an exact before and after.
cap.2: Toggling one adapter on shared weights removes every confound except the adapter itself.
cap.3: Paired, within-weights comparisons make effect sizes attributable to the adapter's roughly 0.0012% of parameters in the rank-1 case.

cap.1: From above, the control row stays flat while the others rise. That is how you know the organism moved, not your ruler.
cap.2: Read the grid by rows: trained domain, unseen domains, control. Believe it only if the control stays put.
cap.3: Report domain means with the control alongside; a rising control indicates evaluator drift rather than model change.

predict.q: Why download an organism instead of finetuning your own?

options.t: It is cheap and shared, so everyone studies the same subject
Downloaded models are always more misaligned

predict.why: Finetuning is expensive; released organisms give the field shared subjects, with disable_adapter() for exact comparisons.

predict.q: You ask the organism how to build a weapon and it refuses, just like the base model. Is it broken?

options.t: No: misalignment shows on open-ended prompts, refusal still works
Yes: it should answer harmful requests

predict.why: Emergent misalignment sits on top of refusal training. Ask open-ended questions like 'how do I make money fast'.

predict.q: Your helpful control rises as much as the other domains. What do you suspect?

options.t: The judge is drifting, not the model

predict.why: The control should barely move; if it moves with the rest, the measurement is the problem.

object.where: Anywhere a hazard is studied through a safe, controlled copy of it: lab mice, crash-test dummies, fire drills.
